|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Post-atomization — collect powder from atomizer** | No peer-reviewed arm-based implementation located for rePOWDER or comparable small metal-atomizer collection. Published work discusses powder recycling and sieving, not autonomous collection. | **No published throughput, success, recovery, or contamination result found.** | Powder adhesion, inaccessible collector geometry, spills, airborne combustible dust, and alloy-to-alloy cleaning remain unquantified. | **Conditional.** The arm can move a sealed collector under 1.5 kg; open pouring should instead occur in a purpose-built grounded, contained transfer station. Do not place the arm in the atomizer chamber. |
| **1. Post-atomization — load/unload sieve stack; classify six fractions** | Commercial sieve shakers automate vibration, but no peer-reviewed robotic loading/unloading workflow with alloy-development metrics was located. Von Rohr notes that automated grinding and sieving have partially available commercial solutions requiring adaptation (pqac-00000062). | **No published robotic success rate, recovery, cycle time, or cross-alloy carryover result found.** | A six-sieve stack plus 250–300 g powder may exceed payload; lids and pans can jam; retained powder adheres to mesh; cleaning and carryover dominate validation. | **Partial.** Arm can handle individual lightweight sieves, lids, and jars with fixtures; use a powered lift/clamp and stationary shaker for an assembled stack. |
| **1. Post-atomization — riffle/split powder** | No peer-reviewed robotic riffler or rotary splitter integrated into an AM-alloy loop was located. | **No published splitting precision, recovery, or contamination result found.** | Representative sampling requires controlled feed rate and validated increment geometry; cleaning inaccessible chutes between alloys is difficult. | **Reachable with dedicated equipment.** Arm can load a sealed rotary splitter or actuate indexed containers; freehand pouring is unlikely to be sufficiently repeatable. |
| **1. Post-atomization — mass balance of fractions** | Analytical balances and robot transport are mature; A-Lab and AlloyBot demonstrate robot-to-balance workflows, although not atomized-powder mass balance (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000026). | AlloyBot weighing is typically under 0.5 h per multielement charge; steady-state synthesis is about one alloy h⁻¹ (pqac-00000012). **No powder-recovery validation reported.** | Static charge, powder on vessel exteriors, drafts, balance settling, and tare/container identity must be controlled. | **High.** Use capped standardized cups, balance-door automation, AprilTag/2D-code identity, and repeated gross/tare measurements. |
| **1. Post-atomization — jar, cap, label, and inventory fractions** | No peer-reviewed implementation located for robotic jarring and labelling of combustible AM metal powders. General autonomous labs demonstrate vial/rack transport (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). | **No published success, throughput, recovery, or cross-contamination metrics found.** | Screw-cap torque, liner seating, label adhesion, powder on threads, and identity reconciliation require validation. | **High for sealed jars.** Use keyed nests, low-torque caps or preassembled septum lids, barcode printing, and machine-readable verification; avoid manipulating loose powder directly. |
| **1. Post-atomization — prepare and seal O/N/H aliquots** | No peer-reviewed robotic workflow located for weighing and hermetically sealing metal-powder aliquots for inert-gas-fusion O/N/H analysis. | **No published cycle time, seal-failure rate, blank, or cross-contamination result found.** | Tiny aliquots, static, capsule folding/crimping, contamination blanks, and chain of custody are unresolved. | **Dispensing is conditional; sealing generally needs dedicated tooling.** Use a grounded enclosed dispenser plus pneumatic/electric crimper; the arm can transport capsules and sealed vials. |
| **2. Characterization — disperse powder onto SEM stub** | **EMSBot**, Milsted et al. 2025: modified 3D printer, vacuum pickup, carbon-tape stubs, and electrostatic deposition (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004). | Demonstrated at 10 kV, 10 mA, 5 s exposure; pickup is retried three times before requesting a human. Dispersion was more uniform and less agglomerated than manual preparation, but no aggregate throughput or success percentage was reported (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003). | High voltage and airborne-particle containment require redesign for combustible aluminium; deposition is particle-size selective and chemistry dependent. | **High for stub logistics; do not copy open electrostatic deposition for Al without a formal ignition-risk review.** A grounded, enclosed mechanical/vacuum dispersion module is preferable. |
| **2. Characterization — automated SEM imaging and particle-shape analysis** | DeCost et al. 2016 established autonomous computer-vision characterization; Bakas et al. 2022 reported Mask R-CNN powder segmentation. **AutoEMX/AutoEMXSp**, Giunto et al. 2025–2026, automates particle localization, EDS spots, spectral filtering, and phase clustering (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000050). | AutoEMX typically acquires about 100 spectra in 20–45 min per sample, processes tens of samples per day, and achieved compositions generally within 5–10% relative deviation across 74 samples and 38 elements (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000053). | Requires instrument API access and good dispersion; particles below roughly 2 µm are disfavoured; irregular geometry and substrate contamination still cause rejected spectra. | **High for stub exchange if the SEM has an automatable load lock; analysis is software-side.** Payload is not limiting. |
| **2. Characterization — introduce sample to laser-diffraction particle sizer** | Autosamplers and wet-dispersion units exist commercially, but no peer-reviewed arm-integrated metal-alloy workflow with recovery or carryover metrics was located. | **No relevant published robotic success rate or cycle time found.** | Representative subsampling, wet versus dry dispersion, ultrasound-induced deagglomeration, solvent compatibility, and complete line cleaning can bias PSD results. | **High for sealed-vial loading.** Use the instrument’s enclosed autosampler; avoid arm-based open pouring or aerosol-generating dry feed. |
| **2. Characterization — Hall/Carney flowability** | Published studies compare standardized manual funnels and automated rheometers; they do not report autonomous sample loading and cleaning. | No robotic metric found. Test results are method- and powder-dependent; standardized funnel tests can fail to flow for cohesive powders. | Start detection, funnel blockage, complete recovery, cleaning, humidity, and operator tapping strongly affect results. | **Moderate.** Arm can place a cup and actuate a gate; funnel filling, levelling, recovery, and cleaning should be enclosed and fixture-driven. |
| **2. Characterization — apparent and tap density** | Commercial tap-density instruments automate tapping/counting, but no peer-reviewed end-to-end robotic AM-powder workflow was located. | **No published robotic cycle time, success rate, or cross-contamination result found.** | Standardized filling, avoiding pre-compaction, reading volume, cleaning cylinders, and powder recovery remain manual. | **High for instrument tending.** Use lightweight keyed cylinders, machine vision for meniscus/bed height, and sealed transfer fixtures. |
| **3. Solid specimens — remove LPBF parts from build plate** | Industrial bandsaw, wire-EDM, and robotic machining cells automate removal, but no alloy-discovery-loop paper with general success and cycle metrics was located. | **No transferable success rate or cycle-time evidence found.** | Cutting loads, heat, swarf, supports, geometry variation, plate mass, and collision risk exceed benchtop-arm capabilities. | **Industrial equipment required.** The PiPER may tend small loose coupons after separation, not perform sawing, EDM, or high-force support removal. |
| **3. Solid specimens — section specimens** | Automated abrasive saws are commercially mature, but published closed-loop robotic loading metrics for AM alloy campaigns were not located. | **No relevant success-rate or cycle-time dataset found.** | Cutting force, coolant, guarding, clamping, blade wear, and geometry-specific fixturing dominate. | **Arm tending only.** A guarded automatic saw with pneumatic vise is required; robot should handle only lightweight, pre-fixtured samples. |
| **3. Solid specimens — hot/compression mounting** | Automated mounting presses exist commercially; no peer-reviewed robot-integrated AM-alloy workflow with measured reliability was located. | **No published robotic metric found.** | Typical mounting forces and temperatures are far beyond the arm; resin dosing and mould cleaning add contamination risks. | **Industrial press required.** Arm can load moulds/coupons using fixtures but cannot supply pressing force; cold-mount dispensing is more accessible. |
| **3. Solid specimens — grind, polish, clean, etch, and image** | **RASI**, BAM: UR5e, modified Qpol250 BOT, cleaning/etching station, and automated microscope; Lemiasheuski et al. 2023 and Moschetti et al. 2025 (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). | Up to 150 slices per specimen per day; largely unattended 24/7 operation; samples to about 15 × 15 × 15 mm³; z spacing to about 0.17 µm. Position variation is submicrometre laterally and below 1° rotationally (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016). | Throughput decreases with extensive polishing, etching, or imaging; requires dedicated grinder/polisher, kinematic holders, fluid handling, and substantial integration. | **Transport feasible; polishing force is not.** PiPER can shuttle standardized pucks, but the grinder/polisher must clamp and apply load independently. |
| **3. Solid specimens — Vickers/microhardness** | Commercial automatic stages perform autofocus, indentation arrays, and image measurement; no peer-reviewed arm-loaded AM-alloy loop with reliability metrics was located. | **No published end-to-end loading success or cycle time found.** | Surface finish, focus, edge spacing, indentation recognition, and specimen tilt dominate error. | **High for puck loading** if the tester has an automatic stage and repeatable nest; the indenter supplies force. |
| **3. Solid specimens — Archimedes density** | No peer-reviewed robotic air/weighed-liquid density workflow for AM coupons was located; published AM studies generally report manual Archimedes measurements. | **No published robotic cycle time or success rate found.** | Trapped bubbles, wetting, suspension-wire contact, temperature, evaporation, open porosity, drying, and droplets on the balance cause failures. | **Moderate.** Feasible with a dedicated air/liquid balance, fixed basket, wetting protocol, drip tray, and automated drying—not by freehand robot motion alone. |
| **3. Solid specimens — load tensile coupons** | Universal test frames automate control and data acquisition, but no peer-reviewed flexible robot-loading system for AM ASTM E8 sub-size coupons with measured success was located. | **No published success rate or loading cycle found.** | Grip alignment, extensometer attachment, specimen identification, fractured-half retrieval, and pinch/crush hazards are unresolved. | **Conditional.** Arm can place light coupons into open self-centering grips; fixture actuation and alignment sensing must be provided by the test frame. |
| **4. Charge preparation — weigh powders/pieces** | **AlloyBot**, Selvaraj/Boonpetch 2026 preprint: robot, pellet dispensers, wire cutters, balance, and reusable copper crucibles (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). **Jiang et al. 2023**: dual-arm biomimetic spatula/balance dispensing (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000042). **A-Lab** uses an automatic Quantos dispenser balance (pqac-00000026). | AlloyBot: approximately one alloy h⁻¹ in steady state, <0.5 h typical weighing, better than 1 at.% target accuracy, and measured compositions within EDX’s ±1 at.% uncertainty; no overall success percentage (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012). Jiang: 0.07% mean error, 0.56% SD for non-challenging solids at 200 mg, but 23.1% aggregate failure; 239–552 s for NaNO₂ robot dispenses (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000043). | AlloyBot evidence is a **2026 preprint**; Jiang failures include blocked outlets, deliquescence, sticking, and balance-detection errors. Neither validates combustible Al-powder containment. | **Pieces/slugs: high. Powders: conditional.** A low-payload arm can move cups, pellets, wire and small master-alloy pieces; use enclosed gravimetric dispensing for loose Al powder. |
| **4. Charge preparation — kit and load crucible/atomizer cup** | AlloyBot robotically pours weighed elemental charges into copper crucibles and orders lower-melting elements beneath higher-melting elements (pqac-00000007). | Handles alloys up to 25 cm³ and over 100 g Ti-6Al-4V; load-lock permits melting to begin within 15 min and production of 24 alloys day⁻¹, with about 45 min daily crucible cleaning (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011). | Not demonstrated for press-fit 6063 cups/plugs, rePOWDER loading, or aluminium-powder charges; press-fitting itself may require force tooling and dimensional verification. | **High for kitting and placement.** The arm can load 250–300 g charges and cups; use a guided arbor/pneumatic press for plugs and a separate force sensor or go/no-go gauge. |
| **5. Safety — combustible metal powder and autonomous robotics** | The SDL safety literature recommends RAMP/hierarchy-of-controls, authorization, monitoring, emergency stops, collision detection, constrained motion, human review, and near-miss reporting, but gives no metal-dust-specific NFPA/ATEX implementation (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). A-Lab limited campaigns to air-stable targets and operated in air rather than proving inert-powder handling (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023). | **No published success/incident rate for robots handling open combustible Al powder found. No peer-reviewed validation against NFPA 484/660 or ATEX found.** | NFPA 660/484 and the adopted fire/electrical codes require a project-specific combustible-dust hazard analysis; relevant engineering issues include ignition-capable electrical/mechanical equipment, bonding/grounding, dust-tight containment, housekeeping, ventilation/collection, explosion protection or inerting, and safe isolation. Exact obligations depend on dust explosibility data, quantity, occupancy, and authority having jurisdiction. | **Do not expose an ordinary PiPER/Raspberry Pi system to classified open-powder space without AHJ-approved design.** Prefer sealed grounded containers and a negatively contained or inert glovebox/isolator with external actuators; locate nonrated electronics outside. |
| **5. Safety — published incidents and autonomous-lab practice** | Leong et al. call for systematic near-miss reporting and note that SDL safety evidence remains immature (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000033). | **No peer-reviewed incident report involving an autonomous metal-powder lab was located.** Absence of reports is not evidence of safety. | Public descriptions rarely provide hazardous-area classification, dust Kst/Pmax/MIE/MEC values, cleaning validation, or ignition-source assessments. | Implement human authorization for open-powder transitions, interlocked ventilation/inerting, O₂ and pressure monitoring, spill/fire response, and remote shutdown before autonomous operation. |
| **6. Labour/time evidence — powder and alloy-development loops** | McCalla 2023 reviewed semi-automated solid-state powder workflows; A-Lab and AlloyBot provide campaign-level throughput; Von Rohr identifies preparation and characterization as persistent bottlenecks (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000063). | Traditional solid-state synthesis: about 5–10 samples per researcher over three days; conventional Rietveld-quality XRD about 1 h sample⁻¹. A-Lab: 355 experiments and 41 of 58 targets synthesized in 17 days, 71% target success (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000025). AlloyBot: one alloy h⁻¹ with <1 h daily maintenance target. | **No published time-and-motion or person-hour breakdown was located for atomization followed by collection, six-fraction sieving, splitting, jarring, O/N/H sampling, SEM preparation, and flow testing.** The lab’s 10–15 hands-on h run⁻¹ estimate therefore remains plausible but externally unvalidated. | First priority should be direct timing: timestamp every container transition and weigh operation for 10–20 runs, separating hands-on, unattended, cleaning, rework, and safety/PPE time. |
| **7. Overall PiPER deployment judgment** | Existing systems show that low-payload robots are effective chiefly as sample couriers between purpose-built modules: EMSBot for stubs, A-Lab for vessels, and RASI for mounted specimens (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000019). | Demonstrated modules span 5 s electrostatic deposition, 20–45 min automated SEM-EDS, up to 150 metallographic slices day⁻¹, and approximately one automatically weighed/melted alloy h⁻¹ (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000010). | Published systems rarely report recovery, cross-contamination, cleaning effectiveness, or long-run manipulation success—the metrics most important for FLAIME. | **Best near-term scope:** sealed-container logistics, weighing, identity/label verification, SEM-stub handling, instrument tending, and coupon transport. **Use dedicated industrial modules:** sieve-stack lifting, pressing, cutting, mounting, polishing force, tensile gripping, dust containment, and any operation in a classified combustible-dust zone. |


*Table: Step-by-step evidence map for automating a powder-metallurgy and AM alloy-development loop, including measured results, explicit publication gaps, and suitability for BYU’s 1.5 kg PiPER arm. Feasibility ratings distinguish lightweight robotic tending from operations requiring contained or industrial process equipment.*
